issues.legal_issue: A final merits dismissal of a contested writ petition bars the same parties from bringing a later original petition to enforce fundamental rights on the same facts for the same or similar relief.
material_facts: The petitioners had previously sought writ relief from a High Court concerning the same underlying decision and on the same grounds as in their later Supreme Court petitions.

In the relevant prior proceedings, the High Court considered the matters on their merits and dismissed the petitions; in one instance, counsel did not press the petition after the High Court’s prior interpretation of the relevant law had defeated the petitioners’ contentions.
The later petitions sought the same or similar relief on the same facts.
issues.conclusion: The merits decisions bound the parties unless modified or reversed through an appropriate procedure, and the later petitions on the same facts and for the same or similar relief were barred by res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: The general principle of res judicata applies to original petitions under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution. Its foundation is public policy and the rule of law: final decisions of competent courts bind the parties, and a person should not be vexed twice over by the same litigation. The Court relied on the Duchess of Kingston’s case, Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha, and Raj Lakshmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen; it also referred to Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure while explaining that the principle is not confined to its technical requirements. A High Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 may decide the same cause and grant relief of the same character as a petition under Article 32, so its merits decision may bind the parties in the later proceeding.

rule.if: later_original_fundamental_rights_petition and prior_high_court_writ_dismissed_on_merits and same_parties and same_facts_and_same_or_similar_relief

predicates.later_original_fundamental_rights_petiti: A party brings an original court proceeding seeking relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.prior_high_court_writ_dismissed_on_merit: The same party previously brought a contested writ proceeding in a High Court, and the court decided the merits before dismissing it.
predicates.same_parties: The parties to the later proceeding are the same as the parties bound by the earlier decision.
predicates.same_facts_and_same_or_similar_relief: The later proceeding rests on the same facts and seeks the same or similar relief as the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: When a party brings an original fundamental-rights proceeding after a High Court has decided a contested writ proceeding on the merits between the same parties concerning the same facts and relief, the later proceeding is barred.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court’s dismissal of a writ petition for laches or because an alternative remedy is available does not ordinarily bar a later original fundamental-rights petition.
material_facts: The Court considered the effect of High Court dismissals that rested on delay or the availability of an alternative remedy rather than a decision on the merits.
It recognized that facts found in the earlier proceeding may nevertheless be relevant to the later fundamental-rights proceeding.
issues.conclusion: A dismissal for laches or an available alternative remedy is not ordinarily a bar to a later petition, except where facts found by the High Court are themselves relevant to the later proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished a merits judgment, which may create res judicata, from a refusal to issue relief because of laches or an alternative remedy. It applied the general res judicata principle to Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution, while recognizing the different grounds on which a High Court may decline relief under Article 226.

predicates.later_original_fundamental_rights_petiti: A party brings an original court proceeding seeking relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.prior_writ_dismissed_for_laches_or_alter: The party’s earlier writ proceeding was dismissed because of delay or because another effective remedy was available, rather than after a decision on the merits.
predicates.prior_findings_relevant_to_later_claim: Facts found in the earlier proceeding bear on the later fundamental-rights claim.

issues.definition: A later original fundamental-rights proceeding is not barred when the earlier writ was dismissed for delay or an available alternative remedy, unless facts found earlier bear on the later claim.

issues.legal_issue: A non-speaking dismissal in limine or a dismissal after withdrawal does not bar a later original fundamental-rights petition by res judicata.
material_facts: One earlier High Court writ petition was dismissed in limine by an order that stated no reasons.
Another earlier writ petition was withdrawn, and the High Court expressly had not considered its merits.
issues.conclusion: Neither an unexplained dismissal in limine nor a dismissal after withdrawal creates a bar of res judicata to a later petition.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata requires a judicial determination of the rights in controversy and a final decision on them. Without reasons, the basis of an in-limine dismissal cannot safely be identified as a merits determination; withdrawal likewise leaves no decision on the merits. The Court applied the general principle of res judicata to petitions under Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution.

predicates.later_original_fundamental_rights_petiti: A party brings an original court proceeding seeking relief for an alleged violation of fundamental rights.
predicates.prior_writ_dismissed_in_limine_without_r: The earlier writ proceeding was dismissed at the outset without a reasoned order stating the basis for dismissal.
predicates.prior_writ_withdrawn_without_merits_deci: The earlier writ proceeding was withdrawn and the court did not decide the merits.

issues.definition: A later original fundamental-rights proceeding is not barred when the earlier writ was dismissed without reasons at the outset or withdrawn without a merits decision.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights is not merely a discretionary request for relief, and the phrase concerning appropriate proceedings refers to proceedings suited to the order sought.
material_facts: The petitions sought relief for alleged unconstitutional infringements of fundamental rights.
The respondents argued that the right to move the Supreme Court was limited to an appropriate procedure, such as an application for special leave, and that relief under Article 32 was discretionary.
issues.conclusion: The right to move the Supreme Court under Article 32 is itself a fundamental right; appropriate proceedings are those suited to the writ, order, or direction sought, and a petitioner who establishes an illegal or unconstitutional infringement is ordinarily entitled to appropriate relief.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed Article 32(1) as guaranteeing access to the Supreme Court through proceedings appropriate to the nature of the relief sought, not merely to the nature of the case. It relied on Romesh Thappar v. The State of Madras and referred to Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Delhi and Rajasthan. It distinguished the observations in Laxmanappa Hanumantappa Jamkhandi v. Union of India and Dewan Bahadur Seth Gopal Das Mohta v. Union of India as obiter on the asserted discretion to refuse relief.

predicates.fundamental_rights_enforcement_proceedin: A person brings a proceeding seeking enforcement of a fundamental right.
predicates.illegal_or_unconstitutional_fundamental_: The person establishes that a fundamental right has been illegally or unconstitutionally infringed.

issues.definition: A person who establishes an illegal or unconstitutional infringement in a fundamental-rights enforcement proceeding is ordinarily entitled to appropriate relief.
